::: {.callout-note}
**Testing labs** use the main template:
Hypothesis → Visualise → Assumptions → Conduct → Conclude.
:::

## Learning objectives

- Compute a time-dependent Brier score and the Index of Prediction
  Accuracy (IPA).
- Simulate an external-validation cohort with distribution shift and
  evaluate a fitted model on it.
- Describe why a model can have a high internal AUC and a bad
  external IPA.

## Prerequisites

Survival ML from Session 4; calibration from Course 1.

## Background

Validation is the point at which a prediction model either earns its
keep or does not. Internal validation — CV or the bootstrap on the
training data — controls optimism from the fitting step. External
validation applies the fixed model to an independent cohort and
measures discrimination, calibration, and clinical utility. Time-
dependent Brier scores and IPA (1 − Brier/Brier_null) summarise the
cost of a probabilistic prediction at a given horizon, combining
discrimination and calibration into a single number per time.

Real biomedical models routinely lose performance on external cohorts.
Changes in case mix, measurement, baseline risk, or predictor effects can
affect performance in different ways. This lab changes the covariate
distribution while keeping the conditional event model fixed.

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}
TRIPOD-AI asks you to report all three — discrimination, calibration,
clinical utility — on both internal and external data, and to disclose
the shift between them. A reader who only sees AUC on internal data
has no basis for deploying the model.
:::

## Setup

```{r}
#| label: setup
library(tidyverse)
library(survival)
library(pROC)
set.seed(42)
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 12))
```

## 1. Hypothesis

A Cox model fit on a development cohort retains its calibration and
discrimination on an external cohort with shifted covariate
distribution.

## 2. Visualise

```{r}
make_cohort <- function(n, mu_x = 0, beta = 0.6) {
  x <- rnorm(n, mu_x)
  lp <- beta * x
  t <- rexp(n, rate = exp(lp - 1))
  c <- rexp(n, rate = 0.1)
  time <- pmin(t, c)
  event <- as.integer(t <= c)
  tibble(x = x, time = time, event = event)
}
dev  <- make_cohort(500, mu_x = 0)
ext  <- make_cohort(500, mu_x = 1.0)   # distribution shift
bind_rows(dev |> mutate(cohort = "dev"),
          ext |> mutate(cohort = "ext")) |>
  ggplot(aes(x, fill = cohort)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, alpha = 0.7, position = "identity")
```

## 3. Assumptions

Censoring is independent of both event time and covariates in this simulation.
We use marginal inverse-probability-of-censoring weights (IPCW), require
positive censoring survival at the horizon, assume Cox proportional hazards,
and use no time-varying covariates. Subjects censored before the horizon
have unknown outcomes and are not coded as event-free.

## 4. Conduct

Fit on dev; predict survival at a fixed horizon on both cohorts.

```{r}
fit <- coxph(Surv(time, event) ~ x, data = dev)
horizon <- 3

# Match the mean-centred baseline hazard to the same prediction reference.
# This helper is for the unstratified, fixed-covariate model used in this lab.
predict_surv <- function(fit, newdata, t) {
  bh <- basehaz(fit, centered = TRUE)
  stopifnot(length(t) == 1, is.finite(t), t >= 0, t <= max(bh$time))
  H0 <- c(0, bh$hazard)[findInterval(t, bh$time) + 1L]
  lp <- predict(fit, newdata = newdata, type = "lp", reference = "sample")
  exp(-H0 * exp(lp))
}

# Marginal IPCW is valid here because censoring is independent of X and T.
# Censoring that depends on predictors needs a conditional censoring model.
horizon_weights <- function(data, t) {
  g <- survfit(Surv(time, 1 - event) ~ 1, data = data)
  g_before <- c(1, g$surv)[findInterval(data$time, g$time, left.open = TRUE) + 1L]
  g_at <- c(1, g$surv)[findInterval(t, g$time) + 1L]
  cases <- data$event == 1 & data$time <= t
  controls <- data$time > t
  if (g_at <= 0 || any(g_before[cases] <= 0))
    stop("Insufficient censoring support at this horizon")
  weights <- numeric(nrow(data))
  weights[cases] <- 1 / g_before[cases]
  weights[controls] <- 1 / g_at
  list(cases = cases, controls = controls, weights = weights)
}

score_horizon <- function(data, p_event, t) {
  stopifnot(length(p_event) == nrow(data), all(is.finite(p_event)),
            all(p_event >= 0 & p_event <= 1))
  w <- horizon_weights(data, t)
  brier <- mean(w$weights * (as.numeric(w$cases) - p_event)^2)
  km <- survfit(Surv(time, event) ~ 1, data = data)
  null_risk <- 1 - c(1, km$surv)[findInterval(t, km$time) + 1L]
  null_brier <- mean(w$weights * (as.numeric(w$cases) - null_risk)^2)
  # Cumulative/dynamic AUC: observed cases by t against survivors beyond t.
  auc <- NA_real_
  if (any(w$cases) && any(w$controls)) {
    order_control <- order(p_event[w$controls])
    control_risk <- p_event[w$controls][order_control]
    cumulative_weight <- c(0, cumsum(w$weights[w$controls][order_control]))
    below <- cumulative_weight[findInterval(p_event[w$cases], control_risk,
                                           left.open = TRUE) + 1L]
    at_or_below <- cumulative_weight[findInterval(p_event[w$cases], control_risk) + 1L]
    auc <- sum(w$weights[w$cases] * (below + .5 * (at_or_below - below))) /
      (sum(w$weights[w$cases]) * sum(w$weights[w$controls]))
  }
  c(auc = auc, brier = brier,
    ipa = if (null_brier > 0) 1 - brier / null_brier else NA_real_)
}

s_dev <- predict_surv(fit, dev, horizon)
s_ext <- predict_surv(fit, ext, horizon)
metrics_dev <- score_horizon(dev, 1 - s_dev, horizon)
metrics_ext <- score_horizon(ext, 1 - s_ext, horizon)
b_dev <- unname(metrics_dev["brier"]); b_ext <- unname(metrics_ext["brier"])
ipa_dev <- unname(metrics_dev["ipa"]); ipa_ext <- unname(metrics_ext["ipa"])
auc_dev <- unname(metrics_dev["auc"]); auc_ext <- unname(metrics_ext["auc"])
rbind(development_apparent = metrics_dev, external = metrics_ext)
```

A calibration plot at the horizon.

```{r}
mk_cal <- function(p, data, lab, t) {
  breaks <- unique(quantile(p, seq(0, 1, by = .2)))
  bin <- if (length(breaks) > 1) cut(p, breaks, include.lowest = TRUE) else factor(rep(1, length(p)))
  bind_rows(lapply(split(seq_along(p), bin), function(i) {
    km <- survfit(Surv(time, event) ~ 1, data = data[i, ])
    # Do not extend a group's observed risk beyond its follow-up support.
    observed <- if (max(data$time[i]) >= t) {
      1 - c(1, km$surv)[findInterval(t, km$time) + 1L]
    } else NA_real_
    tibble(cohort = lab, mean_pred = mean(p[i]), obs = observed)
  }))
}
bind_rows(mk_cal(1 - s_dev, dev, "development (apparent)", horizon),
          mk_cal(1 - s_ext, ext, "external", horizon)) |>
  ggplot(aes(mean_pred, obs, colour = cohort)) +
  geom_point() + geom_line() +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, colour = "grey50") +
  labs(x = "Predicted event probability at horizon",
       y = "Kaplan–Meier event probability within prediction groups")
```

## 5. Concluding statement

> At horizon 3, the independent simulated external cohort had
> cumulative/dynamic AUC `r round(auc_ext, 2)`, IPCW Brier score
> `r round(b_ext, 3)`, and IPA `r round(ipa_ext, 2)`. Apparent development
> values were AUC `r round(auc_dev, 2)`, Brier `r round(b_dev, 3)`, and
> IPA `r round(ipa_dev, 2)`. Development estimates reuse training data and
> therefore do not constitute internal validation.

Only the distribution of X changes here; the conditional event-time model
is unchanged. Such covariate shift need not cause miscalibration. Brier,
AUC, and the cohort-specific null model used for IPA may change with case
mix even when predictions remain calibrated. The grouped calibration plot
is descriptive and has sampling uncertainty; it does not establish a
systematic direction of error in every simulation.

::: {.notes}
Mention that recalibration (update the baseline hazard or the
intercept of a logistic model) often fixes calibration without
retraining the whole model.
:::

## Common pitfalls

- Reporting AUC as the only discrimination metric on an external
  cohort.
- Ignoring censoring when computing a Brier score at a horizon;
  `pec` or `riskRegression` handle this properly.
- Recalibrating on external data and then reporting the resulting
  performance as external validation.

- Kattan MW, Gerds TA (2018), *The index of prediction accuracy: an
  intuitive measure useful for evaluating risk prediction models*.
- Steyerberg EW, *Clinical Prediction Models*, ch. 15–17.
